title: HakoVM – Firecracker-class VMs in macOS, built by a macOS hacker
description: HakoVM: Firecracker-class microVMs for macOS, built for AI agents. One binary on Apple's Containerization framework. - las7/HakoVM
fullText:
Firecracker-class microVMs for macOS. Built for AI agents.

Install · For agents · vs Docker / Apple container / Lima · Design · Performance · Roadmap

Boot a hardware-isolated Linux VM from any OCI image in about 300 ms, run
commands in it at ~10 ms each, throw it away. No daemon, no Docker, no root.
The guest has no network card unless you give it one.

Full numbers and caveats in docs/comparison.md.

Firecracker needs KVM, so it does not run on a Mac. Docker Desktop, OrbStack
and Lima give you one big shared VM. Apple's container CLI is close, but it
is a general container tool with a daemon and a network stack you may not want.

HakoVM is a thin Swift runtime on Apple's open-source
Containerization framework, shaped
for one job: giving an AI agent a disposable machine it cannot escape from.

Code interpreter. Run model-generated code, get stdout, exit code and files back.
The guest cannot reach the network or any host path you did not mount.

Dependencies. The guest is offline by default. Install once with
--network and commit the result; every later run boots a copy-on-write
clone of it, offline, in about a second:

Commits layer (--from py-deps --commit py-deps-ml), and ten agents booting
from one commit each get their own clone. Mounting a host venv or
node_modules works too, and so does any image from a registry. See
docs/dependencies.md for when to use which.

Claude Code. Put every Bash call the agent makes inside a VM. Add to
.claude/settings.json:

The project directory is mounted at the same path, so the agent's relative and
absolute paths keep working. HAKO_IMAGE, HAKO_NETWORK=1 and HAKO_MOUNT
tune it. Round trip per command is about 0.7 s including the boot; a warm pool
is next on the roadmap to bring that to the exec latency.

MCP server. One command registers HakoVM as a tool for any MCP client:

The model gets hako_run (command, image or commit, timeout, cwd) and
hako_commits. Network and extra mounts are refused unless you start the
server with --allow-network / --allow-mounts.

Any language. hako run --json --timeout 60 -- ... prints one JSON
object with stdout, stderr, exit code and timings. See
docs/agents.md for all four integration paths and the
patterns that work.

Apple Silicon and macOS 26 or later. No sudo, no developer account.

That drops hako in ~/.local/bin and runs hako setup, which downloads a
28 MB Linux kernel built from Apple's Containerization config and caches
Apple's guest init plus alpine. Everything lives under ~/.hako.

hako is being built around six agent workloads: coding-agent shell, code
interpreter, parallel fan-out, browser agent, eval runs, and hosting untrusted
MCP servers. The design doc describes the primitives that
serve them: profiles, warm pools, host-terminated egress with hostname
allowlists, a credential broker, and commit/fork of prepared rootfs images.

See the roadmap for order and status.

Here's What Lifehacker Readers Think Apple Will Announce on Wednesday
description: Most are betting that Apple will bring back "One more thing."
fullText:
On Wednesday, Apple will finally host its big fall event, and we will likely get our first look at the Apple Watch Series 12, iPhone 18 Pro, and iPhone Ultra, Apple's first foldable iPhone. In the lead-up to this keynote, Lifehacker ran the third and final round of our Big Guessing Game, inviting readers to make predictions about what Apple will announce this week. While we won't know the answers to those questions until Apple officially confirms them during the event, here's a look at what readers think will happen.

The rumors strongly predict that Apple will announce new iPhones and a new Apple Watch on Wednesday, but there's always the possibility of more devices as well. Apple may release new AirPods—with or without embedded cameras—and while there's a chance they'll announce new Macs, I'm skeptical, given that Apple surprised us all with Mac news last week.

My first question of the third round of the Big Guessing Game was about which of these products Apple would announce first. (To be clear, we posted the quiz before Apple's surprise Mac announcements.) The majority of respondents (49%) believe Apple will start with its iPhone news, while 23% believe the company will kick things off with Apple Watch. Smaller percentages believe Apple will focus on other products first: 16% think they'll announce new Macs first (sorry!), while 12% think AirPods will get the first shoutout.

Wednesday's keynote will be Apple's first with a new CEO since the iPhone 4S event back in 2011. Tim Cook is no longer head of Apple; as such, new Apple CEO John Ternus will lead this week's event. That said, Apple events feature numerous employees throughout, and since Tim Cook is still Apple's executive chair, it stands to reason Cook could make an appearance on Wednesday.

Lifehacker readers were pretty split on this question, though there was a clear majority. 55% of respondents think Cook will make an appearance, while 45% believe he will not. I could see the logic behind both: It might only make sense for Cook to "pass the baton" to Ternus, so to speak. On the other hand, Apple might want to establish the new "Ternus" era, and featuring Cook may muddy the waters.

The iPhone Ultra will likely steal the show on Wednesday. It'll be Apple's first foldable iPhone, will likely cost over $2,000, and will possibly be delayed. To that point, I asked Lifehacker readers when the iPhone Ultra's preorder will actually open up. Most are optimistic, with 43% responding that iPhone Ultra will be available to preorder this month. Another 33% think Apple will open up preorders in October, while 15% think the Ultra will be unavailable until November. A final 9% think Apple will open preorders in another month entirely.

Apple events are rarely short. The company typically has a lot of announcements to get through, and even though these keynotes are now pre-recorded, they can run for as long as a feature-length movie. However, there's no set runtime for Apple events, which makes it a perfect guessing-game question.

The majority (51%) of Lifehacker readers think that Apple's keynote will run 90 to 120 minutes long; 41% think that the event will be a bit shorter, running from 60 to 90 minutes; and a slim respondent pool (8%) thinks that Apple's event will be long, running more than two hours. I don't think that's likely, but it's not impossible—maybe Apple will go quite in-depth on that foldable iPhone.

"One more thing" was an Apple event staple for years, made famous by then-CEO Steve Jobs. The company would save a huge announcement for the end of the show and introduce it by saying "One more thing." It would be a fun nod for Ternus to bring back the slogan, but, again, perhaps the new CEO wants to carve his own path. Most Lifehacker readers think he'll do it, though: 61% think "One more thing" is coming back this year, compared to 39% who don't. Personally, I hope he does it, and I hope that whatever gets announced is actually surprising, and not something that's been leaked already.

fullText:
Student protesters among those hacked, says digital rights group, though Aleksandar Vučić’s government denies spying

At least 14 people from across Serbian civil society were targeted with advanced spyware earlier this year in what the digital rights group Share Foundation said was the largest documented ​wave of such infection in Serbia to date.

The wave of spyware infections was discovered in August after Apple notified people in 110 ⁠countries that they had probably been victims ⁠of mercenary spyware.

The Citizen Lab, which carries out forensic analyses of spyware attacks, released an analysis on Wednesday showing that at least one of the Serbians had been targeted with the NSO Group’s Pegasus spyware, which would have given the attacker “total access to the device”.

Share said those targeted included members of a Serbian student movement that has been a thorn in the side of the government of Aleksandar Vučić since 2024. Coalescing out of countrywide protests that followed the collapse of a train station that winter, it is one of the largest student movements in Europe.

Vučić has been in power for more than a decade, during which time critics have said he has overseen a hollowing-out of institutions while steering the country closer to Moscow.

There is no evidence that Vučić’s government was the entity that targeted the student with the Pegasus spyware. However, other spyware used against the students, including a software called NoviSpy, has been previously connected to Serbian authorities.

In an interview with Euronews Serbia TV on Wednesday, Ana Brnabić, the parliamentary speaker and a ranking member of the ruling Serbian Progressive party, denied that students had been spied on. “Absolutely not,” she said. “I do not believe a single word they’ve [students, Share] said.”

Share said the timing – during March’s local elections – may have been a practice run before snap elections set for this October.

“This is the largest documented wave of surveillance in Serbia so far,” said Andrijana Ristic, a policy adviser at Share. “We imagine … that the local elections were basically used as a test for the ruling party to see [the spyware’s] strengths, but also to see the amount of pressure they are able to exert over the students and the opposition.”

John Scott-Railton, a senior researcher at the Citizen Lab, said: “Our forensic findings, and this fresh wave of Apple threat notifications reveal that Serbia’s peaceful pro-democracy movement is being aggressively targeted with mercenary spyware ahead of key 2026 election cycles.”

Milica Popović, one of the students who was targeted, called the attacks “cruel”. She said: “Thinking that someone may have entered my private space without my knowledge made me feel so exposed.”

But, she said, the attack, as uncomfortable as it was, would not deter her or the student movement. “If their intention was to frighten us, or make us stop, it will not work.”

NSO Group, which makes Pegasus, a spyware that has been leveraged by authoritarian states to target journalists, human rights campaigners and dissidents, began as an Israeli company with close ties to the military.

It is now under US ownership, and appears to be searching for a way into the US market, including through efforts to get off the US Commerce Department’s blacklist. However, this and other incidents will raise questions about what has been described as their attempt to rebrand as an “ethical spyware company”.

NSO Group has been permanently barred by a US court from targeting WhatsApp users and Meta products. It is unclear if this most recent Pegasus attack happened via WhatsApp.

“Today, Pegasus is still being used to hack people campaigning for democracy. NSO spent a decade promising reform, yet their spyware is still an instrument of political repression,” said Railton.

NSO Group was approached for comment.

title: Tim Cook stepped down as Apple CEO, but the ‘Trump whisperer’ isn’t going anywhere
description: Cook is giving up Apple’s top job, but his years navigating Trump, tariffs, and China are still valuable enough for the tech giant to keep him close.
fullText:
Tim Cook may be giving up Apple's top job, but the company isn't letting its longtime CEO fall far from the tree just yet.

Cook, who handed the CEO title to longtime hardware chief John Ternus on Tuesday, will stay on as executive chair for the tech company, earning an annual salary of $2 million effective Sept. 26. As chair, Cook will continue assisting with certain aspects of Apple, including "engaging with policymakers around the world," the company said in April when it announced his new role.

Why is Cook staying on as executive chair?

How did Tim Cook become Trump's 'whisperer'?

What manufacturing commitments has Apple made to the US?

What is Tim Cook's new role and compensation at Apple?

Part of the reason Cook may stay on at Apple is that during his 15-year tenure, he became a sort of "Trump whisperer" in navigating the company's relationship with the president. Cook earned the nickname for his ability to strike deals and keep things smooth with the president, as seen through both his tariff negotiations and this year's CEO transition.

Cook even said he'd continue to manage the company's relationship with not only Trump but also the Chinese government, according to Bloomberg. Those relationships have become increasingly important to Apple as its sprawling Asian supply chain puts the company in the middle of Trump's push to use tariffs to bring more manufacturing to the U.S.—and leaves it navigating tensions between Washington and Beijing.

His package won't be limited to the $2 million annual comp either; he was approved for an equity award with a target value of $45 million, according to a regulatory filing.

Cook leaves the CEO job after 15 years at Apple's helm, having taken over shortly before cofounder Steve Jobs' death in 2011. During his tenure, Apple's market capitalization grew from roughly $347 billion to $4.6 trillion, all while increasingly navigating government issues, alongside product and operational challenges.

Cook figured out relatively early how to get Trump's ear.

"He's the one that calls me," Trump told reporters in 2019 when he was asked why he had a good relationship with Cook compared with other tech executives. At the time, tariffs were a problem. Trump said Cook had argued that levies on Apple's China-made products could put the company at a disadvantage against South Korean rival Samsung.

That relationship would be tested again after Trump returned to the White House. In February 2025, Apple announced it would spend $500 billion in the U.S. over four years, including plans to hire 20,000 workers.

But Cook's access to Trump did not mean Apple always got what it wanted. By May 2025, Trump was publicly criticizing Apple as the company expanded iPhone production in India, as part of its efforts to reduce its reliance on China.

fullText:
Tech company submits to controversial Trump order to rename body of water amid US trade spat with Canada

Apple has renamed Lake Ontario as “Lake America” for US users of its Maps app, after an executive order from Donald Trump to change the name of the Great Lake amid his trade spat with Canada.

The Apple Maps app now displays the controversial new name for the lake, which sits between New York state and the Canadian province of Ontario, for users in the US. Apple users outside the country will still see the Lake Ontario name.

Apple had been reportedly mulling whether to submit to Trump’s new order after receiving a personal request from the president for the tech company to change the lake’s name.

Trump welcomed the news, declaring in a Truth Social post that the adoption of “Lake America” by Google Maps and Apple Maps meant the name change was “complete, ratified, and binding”. However, the US cannot compel Canada – or any other country – to also change the name.

The US president officially unveiled the name swap last week. He did not mention his escalating trade feud with the US’s northern neighbors in the order, but the timing suggested a retaliatory move after Canadian officials denounced Trump’s new sweeping tariffs and promised to instate tariffs of their own.

Canada’s prime minister, Mark Carney, rejected the attempt to rename the body of water, saying in a post on social media that the lake’s name comes from the language of the Indigenous Wendat people and predates both the Canadian Confederation and the US Declaration of Independence.

Late last month, trade talks between Washington and Ottawa collapsed, with the US subsequently imposing a 50% tariff on several Canadian imports. Trump additionally threatened another round of 50% duties on Canadian steel, trucks, cars and auto parts to take effect in the new year. Carney retaliated with 25-50% tariffs on hundreds of US goods.

Rather than mention any of this, Trump instead said in the order that the purpose of the renaming is to honor “the policy of my Administration to recognize the extraordinary contributions of the American people and the rich heritage of our history by naming great natural landmarks for our shared achievements”.

Earlier this week, Doug Burgum, the interior secretary, said in an interview with Fox Business that “the president has reached out to Apple directly” and predicted with confidence that US users would “be seeing that change coming up soon”.

Apple’s competitor, Google, already made the change over the weekend, with Google Maps now showing the Lake America branding. Google cited Trump’s order and its practice of using names assigned by the US Geographic Names Information System (GNIS).

In a blogpost issued on Saturday, Google said US users would see the Lake America name while users in Canada will see Lake Ontario, and “those outside of the US and Canada will see both names.”

The digital name change is unsurprising considering Google Maps was an early adopter of the Gulf of America moniker and still currently displays the title, despite the renaming hardly being a success outside US government lingo.

On Tuesday, it was reported that MapQuest, the pioneering online mapping app, reached the No 1 spot on Apple’s App Store after openly rejecting Trump’s request to rename the lake. The app simply posted a screenshot of Lake Ontario on social media last Thursday along with the caption: “We’re not changing it.”

The act of defiance was enough to catapult the app into becoming the most in-demand navigation tool in the US.

title: Tim Cook handed $47m package for new role as executive chair of Apple
description: Pay and shares deal nearly matches $58m award to John Ternus, his successor as CEO at the $4.7tn tech...
fullText:
Pay and shares deal nearly matches $58m award to John Ternus, his successor as CEO at the $4.7tn tech company

Tim Cook has received a $47m (£35m) pay deal as Apple’s executive chair, a remuneration package that nears the level set for his successor as chief executive.

Cook, who handed over to John Ternus on Tuesday, will be paid a base salary of $2m and $45m worth of shares. Half of the share award will be based on performance targets being met, while the remaining half will be paid out over four years.

Ternus will receive a base salary of $3m and a $55m share award, with the latter more weighted to performance.

Cook’s total compensation as chief executive for 2025 exceeded $74m. Cook, who owns more than 3m shares in Apple, has been placed in the multi-billionaire category by Forbes, which estimates his wealth at $3bn.

His predecessor, the Apple co-founder Steve Jobs, was paid a symbolic $1 a year but was worth $7bn when he died, including a sizeable shareholding in Disney he acquired after selling the Pixar animation studio to the entertainment conglomerate.

Cook took over from Jobs in 2011 having impressed as an operations specialist. The stock has risen 2,200% since he took charge, with Apple now valued at about $4.7tn – compared with about $350bn when he became chief executive.

He built the tech company’s sophisticated supply chain and is succeeded by a 51-year-old engineer and longstanding Apple employee, who built products as senior vice-president of hardware engineering.

Ternus’s role meant he ran the engineering teams behind Apple’s entire product lineup, including the iPhones that generate most of the company’s revenue. Analysts are not only anticipating new products but also further progress on integrating AI into Apple hardware.

Ternus’s first big public moment at Apple will be at its annual iPhone event on 9 September, where a foldable handset is expected to be revealed. New iterations of the Apple Watch and AirPods are also anticipated, although Bloomberg reported last week that AirPods with cameras – another big product rumour – “aren’t launching anytime soon”.

Cook’s new mandate includes engaging with policymakers around the world and will involve maintaining the company’s relationship with Donald Trump, as well as overseeing the company’s diplomatic ties with China – a key production hub. In a final memo to employees on Monday, he focused on Apple’s products.

“I will miss leading you and being with you for every step, even as I take enormous comfort in handing the helm to someone as brilliant and wonderful and capable as John,” he said. “Few people understand what it takes to build products that change the world the way John does.”

title: 10 Apple Health Hacks Every iPhone User Should Know
description: You don't need an Apple Watch to get great health insights from Apple.
fullText:
Even if you’ve never opened the Apple Health app, if you have an iPhone, you’ve probably used apps that send information to its on-phone database. Apple Health is a powerful tool for controlling who gets access to your health data, logging data in different ways, and even taking at-home screening tests for certain health issues. If you have an Apple Watch, that’s great, but you don’t need one (or any wearable!) to take advantage of most of these 10 hacks to get more out of the Apple Health app.

Before we get into the other hacks, I’d like to discuss just how private your Apple Health data is (or isn’t). Apple provides its Health privacy policy here, and it says that your data lives on your own device and is encrypted when your phone is locked. There are some exceptions, though, which you can turn on or off. Here are the main things you may want to check on:

Individual apps can ask for permission to read data from Apple Health. (They also need your permission to write data to it.) You can control per-app permissions in Settings. Or, for a specific data point (like “walking and running distance”), go to that area of Apple Health and tap Data Sources and Access.

You can back up your health data via iCloud, which means it will live on Apple’s servers so you can access it from any of your devices. It is encrypted so Apple cannot read it. Manage this from your iCloud settings (in Settings, under your name).

You can share health data with your doctor or with people you know, like family members. To manage who has access, go to the Health app and tap the Sharing tab.

During workouts, some data from your workout may appear in a Live Activity widget on your lock screen. To hide this data while your phone is locked, go to the Settings app, tap Face ID & Passcode, and then under Allow Access When Locked, toggle Workout Health Data.

Your Medical ID may be available when your device is locked. (This is how bystanders and first responders can access your emergency contact or other information you’d like to remain available in emergencies.) To control access to this, go to the Health app, find Medical ID, and toggle Show When Locked.

The Health app includes a built-in medication tracker with a number of hidden features. Browse or search for Medications, and set up tracking by adding a medication, or anything else. You can type in the name, or use your camera to scan the bottle’s label. (This also works for over-the-counter meds and supplements, like if you want to be sure to take a vitamin every day.) I like that you can customize a pill-shaped icon to match a pill’s appearance.

Next, you can set up reminders. From this screen, you can tell the app when you plan to take your medication (if it’s one you take regularly, rather than as needed). The Health app will notify you at that time. To make the most of this feature, I recommend setting up follow-up reminders, which you’ll find on a different screen as well—more about that below.

After you set up your medications, scroll to the bottom of the medications screen and tap Pin to Summary. Now you just have to open the Health app and tap Medications to see a list of what you need to take today. You can also log via Siri, including batched logging like “Siri, log that I took my 10 a.m. meds” so you don’t have to list each one.

At the bottom of the Medications screen, you can tap Options and turn on Follow Up Reminders, which will give you an extra notification 30 minutes after the first one if you haven’t logged a dose. I use this feature all the time myself: I get the first reminder while I’m in the middle of doing something, eventually take the pill, then the follow-up reminds me to log it. If I got distracted along the way, I have a second chance to not miss a dose.

Another handy feature here is the Export PDF button at the bottom of the page, which will print out a list of all your current medications so you can bring it to your medical appointments or anywhere else you need to.

If you’re not familiar with the Health app, you might not think there’s much there—just a few things on the home screen. You can change that, but it takes a few steps. You see, rather than being a minimalist app, there’s so much available in Health that Apple figures it’s not worth giving you a big list to start off. Tap the magnifying glass icon in the lower right corner, and you’ll see a whole list of categories. You can search from this screen, or browse the categories.

Definitely take a minute to browse through these and see what features you might actually use. If you track what you eat in an Apple Health-connected app, you’ll be able to see all the individual components here: how much protein you’ve gotten today, for instance. Anything that a wearable can track is on here, including things you probably didn’t realize. I have a grade for my walking steadiness, for example.

Once you’ve figured out which of these hundreds of data points are actually useful, put the ones you care about on the main app screen (called Summary). Find a relevant card by searching or browsing, scroll to the bottom, and tap Pin to Summary. This way you can see exactly what you want when you open the app: say, your steps, protein intake, and the day’s medications. (Plus a few things you may want to add after you learn about them below...)

A lot of us are nervous about logging reproductive health data anywhere that may not be private. I’ve written that Euki may be the best standalone app for privacy, but you don’t need to use an app at all: Tracking directly in Apple Health means that your data is encrypted and lives on your phone, subject to the privacy features discussed above.

To use the built-in tracker, go to the magnifying glass and tap (or search for) Cycle Tracking. The cycle tracker on this screen (which you can pin to your summary) allows you to log menstrual bleeding, as well as “factors” like contraceptive use, pregnancy, and more.

Under the Options at the bottom of this screen, you can turn on period predictions, fertile window estimates, and more. I recommend enabling the Symptoms log if you’d like to keep track of things like cramps and nausea. You can also decide if you want Apple Health to use your temperature and heart rate data from a wearable for better cycle detection.

Another surprising use for manual logging in the Health app is under Mental Wellbeing. This is a really useful screen, since it collects things known to affect mental health, like your sleep, exercise minutes, time in daylight, and more. From here, you can also set up emotion and mood logging. The app explains that it considers emotions to be how you feel right now, and moods are how you’ve felt overall that day.

You can turn on reminders to log your moods. The default is to log twice per day: once around midday, and once at the end of the day. Scroll to the bottom of the Mental Wellbeing screen to set up logging.  Once you’ve set it up, it will appear as State of Mind; you may want to pin this to your summary. You can even view graphs of your state of mind over time, and see what other factors they associate with. A really useful view is to tap Show in Charts and then highlight Life Factors so you can see if your moods seem to track your exercise minutes or your hours of sleep.

The Health app also includes a built-in hearing test, but it requires AirPods Pro 3 (or AirPods Pro 2). To find the hearing test, look up Hearing in the Health app, then Get More From Health, and then Take Hearing Test. This will only be available if you have the right type of headphones connected. Follow the prompts to take the test. Apple has more information on this test here. If your results seem concerning, you can export a PDF of your results to discuss with a professional.

Accessing your medical records through patient portals can be annoying. Instead, you can import your digital medical records directly into the Health app, giving you quick access to your medical history as needed. Apple offers a list of the healthcare systems whose data it can access.

It’s worth looking over the privacy policies for this feature as well, but the good news is that the data follows an encrypted connection between your phone and the healthcare organization, without ever giving Apple (the company) access to it. I’d recommend turning off Improve Health Records, which sends an anonymized version of your data to Apple; health records are detailed information about your body—but feel free to leave it on if that’s your preference. You can back up your health data over iCloud, as discussed above.

As with menstrual cycle tracking, it can be useful to any health data directly in the app. You can actually do this with just about any data point: just view that type of data, and then tap the plus sign in the upper right corner. Think you took about 1,000 steps when you had your watch off? Just tap the plus on the Steps screen and add them.

A handy place to use this feature is for blood pressure tracking. Some wearables estimate your blood pressure, like Whoop and the Samsung Galaxy Watch. But you don’t need one of those to log your numbers: just take note of your blood pressure at the doctor’s office, or when you use a wrist cuff or one of those machines they sometimes have at pharmacies. Open Blood Pressure and tap the plus, then put in the new reading. You’ll be able to view your history of blood pressure readings, and even see charts of how it has changed over time.

Some medications affect your heart rate, most notably beta blockers and calcium channel blockers. If you’re taking one of those, your heart rate won’t match Apple’s general-purpose formulas for gauging your cardio fitness (a VO2max estimate) from your heart rate. You’ll appear to have a higher cardio fitness than you actually have.

To let Apple account for this, go to your profile picture, tap Health Details, tap Edit at the top of the page, and scroll down to Medications That Affect Heart Rate. You can select calcium channel blockers or beta blockers, or both; these are the only categories of medication that Apple can account for.

There’s a Medical ID feature that can be accessed from your lock screen even without unlocking your phone. It’s a great place to put your emergency contact information, but to make the most use of it, you need the people in your life to know how to access the information and what’s in there.

I first learned about the Medical ID when I was teaching a class. A student came up to tell me about a medical condition, and showed me how to access her Medical ID (it’s right at the bottom of the lock screen). Most importantly, she made sure I knew what information I’d be able to find there, so I knew when and whether to reach for it in an emergency.

I’d advise that you do the same if you want to be prepared. Besides allergies and contact information, the Medical ID field can include information on whether you’re pregnant, what medications you take, any medical conditions you’d like to disclose, and your height, weight, and blood type. There’s also an area at the bottom for notes, where you can add any information you feel is critical.

Also consider whether you want to turn on Share During Emergency Call, which allows this information to be shared with emergency services. You can also control whether or not your Medical ID appears on your lock screen using a separate toggle.
